rows.source:
We put the first issue of our tiny local history zine together on the library floor, surrounded by photo copies and two kinds of tape. It is now at the printer, which still feels unlikely. The issue has a piece about the old ferry landing, a recipe from the market's first cook, and drawings by the after-school art group. The drawings arrived in an envelope with a note telling us which way was up on each page. That note was useful. We managed to get them all facing the right way in the final layout.

We were hoping for 200 copies, but the current budget covers 120. I wish we could put one in every hand that asked for one, but I also think a modest first run is fine. We will leave copies at the library and the market and share any remaining ones at the open house. I am keeping a list of people who helped with the issue so we can make sure they receive a copy. If we have enough interest, we can look at a second print run later, though nothing is arranged yet.

I am writing to share this exciting milestone and invite everyone to be part of the next chapter of our journey. More practically, we need a couple of people to help fold copies next Thursday evening. It should take about an hour if the printer delivers on Wednesday as promised. If delivery slips, I'll send a note rather than ask people to turn up for nothing. There will be a folding guide, and nobody needs experience. I only ask that we work at a table this time; the library floor has earned a rest.

Thank you to the library staff for letting us borrow the big table so many times, and to everyone who checked dates or hunted down photographs. The work shows in small ways throughout the issue. I am looking forward to seeing the pages as an actual little booklet instead of a stack that slides off my desk.

rows.source:
On the first Friday of each month, we set out a long table in the hall and ask anyone nearby to bring something they have been making. Last time there were knitted mittens, a nearly finished model boat, and a folder of family recipes. The owner of the boat was still deciding how to attach its little mast, and three people offered different ideas. Nobody solved it on the spot, but that was not the point. It was good to see people make room for a question that small and spend time thinking about it together.

You do not have to have a finished piece or know how to explain it. Some people bring the thing they are working on; others bring a photo because the real thing will not fit through the door. Sometimes people just want to see what others are doing. We have had quiet evenings and noisy ones, and both have been good. If you are curious but unsure whether your project counts, it probably does. We have never needed a rule about that.

The next table is this Friday from 5 to 7. Come for a few minutes if that is all you have. We will have tea and a spare corner for projects that need space. Children are welcome with an adult, and it is fine to arrive empty-handed. You can take a seat, look around, and leave whenever you need to. There is no presentation or sign-up sheet, only the table and the people who happen to be there that evening.

A few regulars asked whether they should bring supplies for everyone. That is kind, but there is no need. If you have scraps you were going to throw away and think somebody could use, bring them; otherwise, bring yourself. I hope to see a few familiar faces and some new ones too. The hall can be hard to spot from the road, so follow the path beside the noticeboard and look for the open side door.

Thanks,
[Name]

During the four-week pilot, the help desk resolved 43 of 50 tickets within two business days. That is up from 36 of 50 in the previous four weeks, although the two periods had different mixes of requests. The largest delays in the pilot involved equipment pickups, where staff had to wait for a handoff from the warehouse.

We recommend keeping the daily triage check-in for another month and tracking pickup delays separately. These results suggest the process is helping, but they do not tell us how much of the change came from triage alone.
